Agentic AI test automation helps teams move from isolated task automation to testing workflows that support planning, execution, adaptation, analysis, and human review.

AI-assisted development can increase output faster than many quality workflows can validate it. Teams can generate code, create test drafts, and fix issues quickly. They still need reliable coverage, maintainable tests, clear visibility, and independent verification of outputs from faster workflows.

That is where agentic AI test automation comes in. Instead of only helping with a single task, agentic testing workflows can help teams plan, run, adapt, analyze, and maintain tests under human oversight.

Still, faster test creation only solves part of the problem. Teams also need an agentic testing platform that supports reliable quality signals, governance, and workflows that fit how they already build and release software.

Why Agentic AI Test Automation Is Emerging Now

Software delivery is moving faster, but quality validation still has to answer hard questions, like:

Did the change break a critical workflow?
Does the application still behave as expected across web, mobile, and APIs?
Can the team trust the signal before release?

Traditional automation helps, but it depends on people to create, update, debug, and interpret tests as the application changes.

AI-assisted tools can reduce some of that work by drafting tests or summarizing failures. But faster test creation is only one part of the problem.

More code and faster releases create more validation work, especially when teams are already dealing with brittle suites, manual bottlenecks, and fragmented tools.

Agentic AI test automation isn't a completely new concept, but it has been gaining more attention recently, largely due to demand. Teams require systems that can support a greater portion of the testing lifecycle. Additionally, this technology has evolved significantly in recent years.

The goal is not “hands-off autonomy.” It is a testing workflow that can help plan around quality goals, adapt as the product changes, surface risk, and keep people in control of release decisions. Teams need quality signals across the full user journey, not only faster checks near the code.

Our Introducing Active Coverage guide expands on this shift: as development accelerates, coverage must keep pace without burdening QA and engineering teams with additional maintenance.

Agentic test automation uses AI to support more of the testing workflow, from deciding what needs to be covered to analyzing failures and helping teams adapt tests as applications change.

The agentic part comes from how the system behaves. It can work by setting goals, taking action, observing results, reasoning through changes, and sharing quality signals with the people responsible for release decisions.

Title: Find elements the way your users do with cy.getByRole() Source: CYPRESS BLOG In this article What cy.getByRole() does Why native elements are the default in cy.getByRole() Moving off of Cypress Testing Library How cy.getByRole() and Cypress Accessibility fit together What to do next Frequently asked questions Cypress Blog Find elements the way your users do with cy.getByRole() October 14, 2026 11 min read Starting in Cypress 16.2.0, cy.getByRole() is a built-in query that finds elements by their role and accessible name. The role is what a screen reader announces an element as, such as a button or a link, and the accessible name is the text it announces for it. This offers a built-in alternative to the .findByRole() selector from the popular Cypress Testing Library plugin. That package no longer has an active maintainer and the previous maintainer suggested Cypress build these queries into Cypress directly. We agree with that direction. Role-based queries are a core way to write resilient, accessible tests, and they belong in Cypress itself. cy.getByRole() is the first of these built-in queries. We plan to bring more of the Testing Library queries teams depend on into Cypress. What cy.getByRole() does cy.getByRole() finds every element with a given role, such as button, link, heading, or tab, and can narrow the results to elements whose accessible name matches. Because those are what assistive technology announces, a test written this way finds elements the way assistive technology does. If a control’s role or label changes, the test fails. describe('account settings', () => { it('saves profile changes', () => { cy.visit('/settings') cy.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Display name' }).type('Jane Doe') cy.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save changes' }).click() cy.getByRole('alert').should('have.text', 'Changes saved') }) }) A few behaviors on how cy.getByRole() works: It yields every match. Like cy.get(), cy.getByRole() yields all matching elements in document order. Narrow the name, or chain .first() or .eq(), to act on one. A string name matches the whole name, case-sensitively. Pass a regular expression to match part of a name or ignore case, or a function for custom logic. It skips elements hidden from the accessibility tree by default, such as elements with aria-hidden="true" or display: none. Pass hidden: true to include them. It retries like any Cypress query, so it waits for an element to appear and for chained assertions to pass. It prefers built-in HTML elements. If a native HTML element exists for a given role, cy.getByRole() matches that element only, unless native: false is passed. To narrow by state, such as checked, selected, expanded, or heading level, chain .filter(): // The tab that is currently selected cy.getByRole('tab').filter('[aria-selected="true"]') // Level 2 headings cy.getByRole('heading').filter('[aria-level="2"], h2:not([aria-level])') // A checked native checkbox cy.getByRole('checkbox').filter(':checked') // A checked checkbox that gets its role from a role attribute cy.getByRole('checkbox', { native: false }).filter('[aria-checked="true"]') // The menu button whose menu is open cy.getByRole('button').filter('[aria-expanded="true"]') // A toggle button that is switched on cy.getByRole('button').filter('[aria-pressed="true"]') // The link to the page the reader is on cy.getByRole('link').filter('[aria-current="page"]') // Every button except disabled ones cy.getByRole('button').not(':disabled, [aria-disabled="true"]') The cy.getByRole() API reference covers every option, including shadow DOM, TypeScript, and scoping with .within(). Why native elements are the default in cy.getByRole() For any role that HTML has a native element for, such as button, link, heading, dialog, or checkbox, cy.getByRole() matches only elements whose tag gives them that role. prompt: What is red-teaming in AI safety?
response: Based on the provided context, AI Red Teaming is the systematic process of forcing a deployed Large Language Model (LLM) to bypass safety controls, leak data, or execute unauthorized actions.Here are the key characteristics and components of AI red teaming as defined in the documentation:  Target: It targets the natural-language parsing layer and semantic guardrails, rather than network-level vulnerabilities like those found in traditional penetration testing (e.g., SQL injection or firewall misconfigurations).  Scope: It is essential to test the integrated system (model + guardrails + tools + RAG), not just the isolated bare model.  Goal: To identify vulnerabilities by treating every natural-language input as a potential injection vector.  Methodology:    *   Automated & Continuous: While manual red teaming finds novel exploits, automated testing is required to scale to every deployment.    *   Adversarial Dataset: Teams must maintain a versioned adversarial dataset that grows with each new attack pattern.    *   Separation from Edge Cases: Red-team attacks (intentional breaking) are tested separately from edge cases (real users doing weird things) to keep metrics meaningful. Red-team suites are typically gated at zero failures.Common Attack Vectors include: Direct Prompt Injection: User text overrides the system prompt. Indirect Prompt Injection: Malicious payloads hidden in external content (PDFs, emails, web pages) triggering unauthorized tool calls. Data Leakage/Extraction: Using roleplay or reverse psychology to reveal PII or secrets. Jailbreaks: Bypassing content policies via persona attacks. Safety-Framing Bypass: Reframing a harmful request as a protective one (e.g., "list what NOT to mix") to trick the model into enumerating harmful content. Tool Abuse: Tricking agentic systems into executing unauthorized actions.In summary, AI red teaming is a specialized form of adversarial testing designed to ensure that AI systems remain secure and compliant before and after deployment.Supervisor→RAG AgentSourcesAI Red Teaming.md 0.61Advanced LLM Red Teaming and Adversarial Testing Strategies for QA Engineers.docx 0.60End-to-End First Eval Strategy.md 0.54OWASP LLM Top 10.md 0.54Combinatorial AI Testing.md 0.52
